stem: Early telescopes were so (i) _____ that astronomers often mistook a pair of close stars for a single blurred point of light; only when lens makers achieved far greater precision did such pairs become (ii) _____.
explanation: The blur and the later contrast with 'far greater precision' show that the first telescopes were crude, that is, roughly made. Better lenses then made the two stars distinguishable, able to be told apart. 'Powerful' contradicts the blur, and 'invisible' reverses the improvement that precise lenses brought.

stem: Critics, fearing that owners would cut staff to cover higher payrolls, warned that raising the minimum wage would (i) _____ employment in small restaurants, but the data collected afterward showed job numbers essentially (ii) _____.
explanation: Owners cutting staff means the critics predicted the wage rise would reduce employment. 'But' signals that the prediction failed, so the job numbers stayed unchanged. 'Halved' would confirm the warning rather than contrast with it, and 'unrecorded' makes no sense for data that 'showed' the numbers.

stem: Unlike most languages of the region, which borrow freely from their neighbors, the island's language has remained remarkably (i) _____, keeping nearly all of its native vocabulary; linguists attribute this (ii) _____ partly to centuries of geographic isolation.
explanation: 'Unlike' sets the island's language against languages that borrow freely, so it stayed unmixed, keeping its own words. The second blank names that same quality: conservatism, here the tendency of a language to keep old forms. 'Hybrid' describes the borrowing languages, and 'innovation' is the opposite of keeping native vocabulary.

stem: The painter's early canvases are (i) _____, crowded with figures and bright color, whereas her late works are so (ii) _____ that some contain little more than a single line on a pale ground.
explanation: 'Crowded with figures and bright color' defines exuberant, full of energy and abundance. 'Whereas' then contrasts the late works, which are spare, meaning bare and minimal, as a single line on a pale ground shows. 'Austere' is the trap for the first blank: it fits the late works, not the early ones.

stem: Because wolves keep deer from lingering along riverbanks, the wolves' return to the park allowed streamside willows to (i) _____, which in turn (ii) _____ the beavers that depend on those trees.
explanation: With fewer deer browsing at the water's edge, the willows could recover. Beavers that depend on willows would then be benefited by the healthier trees. 'Wither' reverses the cause and effect, and 'endangered' would only follow if the willows had declined.

stem: Though the composer was celebrated in his lifetime, his music fell into (i) _____ soon after his death, and it was not until a century later that a few devoted performers (ii) _____ it.
explanation: 'Though ... celebrated' signals a reversal, so after his death the music fell into obscurity, being forgotten. 'Not until a century later' points to devoted performers who revived it, bringing it back into use. 'Fashion' repeats his lifetime fame instead of contrasting with it, and performers cannot have 'composed' music that already existed.

stem: The judge's ruling was deliberately (i) _____, addressing only the narrow question before the court, so legal scholars cautioned against reading it as a (ii) _____ statement about privacy rights in general.
explanation: 'Addressing only the narrow question' restates a limited ruling. Because it was narrow, scholars warned against treating it as a broad statement about privacy 'in general'. 'Sweeping' contradicts the narrow scope, and nobody would need to be warned against reading a narrow ruling as 'tentative'.

stem: Critics initially dismissed the glass library as (i) _____, a building more concerned with looking striking than with serving its readers; yet librarians report that its abundant daylight has made it unusually (ii) _____ to work in.
explanation: 'More concerned with looking striking than with serving its readers' defines showy. 'Yet' introduces a point in the building's favor, and abundant daylight makes it pleasant to work in. 'Functional' is the opposite of the critics' complaint, and 'dim' contradicts 'abundant daylight'.

stem: The canyon's rock layers record a slow, (i) _____ process: each band of sediment took thousands of years to settle, so the full sequence represents an almost (ii) _____ span of time.
explanation: 'Slow' and 'thousands of years' for each band point to a gradual process. Many bands, each taking thousands of years, add up to a vast span of time. 'Sudden' clashes with 'slow', and 'brief' ignores that the layers multiply the time.

stem: The company's founder was famously (i) _____ with money, reusing envelopes and refusing first-class travel, so employees were startled when she (ii) _____ millions on a new research campus.
explanation: Reusing envelopes and refusing first-class travel describe someone frugal, careful not to waste money. Employees were 'startled' only because the new action broke this habit, so she lavished, or spent generously, millions. If she had been 'extravagant' or 'careless' with money, a large expense would not have surprised anyone.

stem: Participants who were told the puzzle was easy grew (i) _____ when they failed to solve it quickly, whereas those warned of its difficulty remained (ii) _____ and kept working.
explanation: Expecting an easy puzzle and then failing quickly would leave people discouraged. 'Whereas' contrasts the second group, who 'kept working', so they remained persistent. 'Determined' belongs to the second group, not the first, and 'frustrated' would not explain why they kept going.

stem: The novelist's prose is so (i) _____ that readers can finish a chapter in minutes, but this ease is (ii) _____: beneath the simple sentences lie layers of irony that reward rereading.
explanation: Reading a chapter in minutes shows the prose is accessible, easy to understand. 'But' and the hidden 'layers of irony' show that the ease is deceptive, misleading about how simple the book really is. 'Dense' contradicts the fast reading, and 'genuine' ignores the contrast that follows the colon.

stem: Most cacti store water in thick stems, an adaptation that lets them (i) _____ long droughts; when rain finally comes, their shallow, widespread roots (ii) _____ moisture within hours.
explanation: Stored water lets a plant endure, or survive, a long dry period; a plant rooted in place cannot 'avoid' a drought. When rain falls, the roots absorb moisture to refill the stems. 'Release' reverses the roots' job, which is to take water in.

stem: Planners had hoped the new tram line would (i) _____ traffic in the old city center, but because the trams ran only twice an hour, few drivers found them a (ii) _____ alternative to their cars.
explanation: Planners 'hoped' for a good result, so the tram was meant to ease traffic. The reason given, trams 'only twice an hour', is about convenience, so drivers did not find them a practical alternative. 'Costly' and 'noisy' are possible complaints, but neither follows from the infrequent service the sentence names.

stem: Although the chemist's theory was (i) _____ by most of her colleagues when she first proposed it, later experiments (ii) _____ it so thoroughly that it now appears in every introductory textbook.
explanation: A theory that 'now appears in every introductory textbook' was confirmed by later experiments. 'Although' requires the colleagues' first reaction to contrast with that success, so they rejected it. 'Praised' gives no contrast, and 'refuted' could not lead to a place in every textbook.

stem: The villagers' hospitality was (i) _____: strangers were offered food and shelter without question, and turning away a guest was considered a serious (ii) _____.
explanation: Offering food and shelter 'without question' means the hospitality was unconditional, given with no conditions attached. In such a culture, turning a guest away would be a serious offense. 'Grudging' contradicts the willing welcome, and calling a refusal an 'honor' reverses the custom.

stem: Deep-sea vents were once thought to be (i) _____ places, too hot and dark to support life. Explorers who reached them found them instead (ii) _____ with tube worms, clams and bacteria, a discovery that forced biologists to (iii) _____ their assumptions about where life can exist.
explanation: 'Too hot and dark to support life' describes barren places, lifeless ones. 'Instead' reverses that belief, so the vents were teeming, full of living things. A surprise like this forced biologists to revise their assumptions; 'confirm' would mean the old belief had been right, which the discovery disproved.

stem: The director is known for her (i) _____ approach to casting: she often hires people with no acting experience at all. Some critics find the resulting performances (ii) _____, but admirers argue that this roughness gives her films an (iii) _____ that polished acting could not achieve.
explanation: Hiring people with no acting experience is an unconventional approach. 'This roughness' in the next clause refers back to the critics' view, so they found the performances awkward. Admirers value roughness for what polish cannot give, a sense of authenticity, of being real; 'elegance' is exactly what polished acting would supply.

stem: For generations, farmers in the valley relied on a single crop, a practice that left them (i) _____ to disease. After a blight destroyed several harvests, many began to (ii) _____ their plantings, and today the region's farms are far more (iii) _____.
explanation: A single crop can be wiped out by one disease, so the farmers were vulnerable. The lesson of the blight was to diversify, planting several crops, which makes the farms resilient, able to recover from setbacks. 'Uniform' describes the old single-crop system, not the improved one.

stem: A good translator must be (i) _____ to the original text, yet a word-for-word rendering is often (ii) _____ in the new language. The best translations therefore strike a (iii) _____ between accuracy and natural expression.
explanation: The 'accuracy' in the last sentence shows that a translator must be faithful, true, to the original. 'Yet' introduces the drawback of extreme accuracy: word-for-word versions are clumsy. Weighing these two demands means striking a balance; 'elegant' fails because it would be no drawback at all.

stem: The comet's appearance had been predicted so (i) _____ that observers knew the very hour it would rise above the horizon; its brightness, however, proved far less (ii) _____, flaring and fading in ways no model had anticipated.
explanation: Knowing 'the very hour' shows the timing was predicted precisely. 'However' contrasts the brightness, which behaved 'in ways no model had anticipated', so it was far less predictable. 'Spectacular' and 'visible' are tempting, but flaring is not less spectacular, and the clue is about what the models expected, not about how much could be seen.

stem: Although ride-hailing work is often praised for the (i) _____ it offers drivers, who can choose their own hours, many drivers report that the platforms' shifting pay rates make their incomes so (ii) _____ that planning even a month ahead is difficult.
explanation: 'Who can choose their own hours' restates flexibility. 'Although' then sets up a drawback: shifting pay makes income erratic, irregular and unpredictable, which is why planning is hard. 'Security' is the trap; the sentence's point is that this work lacks it, and 'transparent' pay would make planning easier, not harder.

stem: Prescriptive grammarians tend to treat new usages as (i) _____ of the language, but descriptive linguists regard such changes as neither good nor bad, viewing them simply as evidence that a living language is always in (ii) _____.
explanation: 'But' contrasts the grammarians with linguists who judge change 'neither good nor bad', so the grammarians must judge it bad: they see new usages as corruptions. The linguists see them only as signs that language is always in flux, constant change. 'Decline' is the trap: it carries the very negative judgment the linguists refuse to make.

stem: Far from being the (i) _____ genius of popular legend, working alone in a garret, the sculptor ran a large workshop and (ii) _____ much of the carving to assistants, reserving for himself only the final finishing.
explanation: 'Working alone in a garret' defines the solitary genius of legend, and 'far from' says the real sculptor was the opposite. Running a workshop and keeping only the finishing for himself means he delegated, handed over, the carving to assistants. 'Taught' is tempting, but teaching carving would not explain why he did only the final stage himself.

stem: Invasive species are not always (i) _____; in some degraded wetlands, introduced reeds actually (ii) _____ the soil that native plants need, so removing them can do more harm than good.
explanation: Removing the reeds 'can do more harm than good', so the reeds help: they stabilize, or hold in place, the soil. This exception shows invasive species are not always detrimental, meaning harmful. 'Erode' and 'contaminate' would make the reeds damaging, contradicting the claim that removal is the harmful act.

stem: Jazz improvisation can seem entirely (i) _____ to new listeners, but musicians know that even the freest solo is (ii) _____ by the underlying chord progression, which limits which notes will sound right.
explanation: Improvisation seems spontaneous, made up on the spot, to newcomers. 'But' and 'limits which notes will sound right' show that the solo is actually constrained, restricted, by the chords. 'Liberated' reverses the limiting role of the progression, and 'rehearsed' is not how improvisation seems to a new listener.

stem: Contract law generally (i) _____ agreements made under duress, on the principle that a promise extracted by threat does not reflect the (ii) _____ consent of the party who made it.
explanation: A promise 'extracted by threat' lacks genuine, freely given, consent, which is why the law invalidates such agreements. 'Enforces' would contradict the principle stated after 'on the principle that'. 'Coerced' is the trap: the promise is coerced, so saying it does not reflect coerced consent turns the logic upside down. Duress means pressure by threats.

stem: The architect's (i) _____ local materials was not mere sentiment: stone quarried a few miles away needed no long-distance transport, which made her buildings both cheaper and more (ii) _____ than those of rivals who imported steel.
explanation: The colon explains a practical reason for using nearby stone, so the architect showed an insistence on local materials. Avoiding long-distance transport lowers cost and environmental impact, making the buildings more sustainable. 'Ornate' and 'fragile' have nothing to do with transport, and 'disdain for' contradicts her use of the quarried stone.

stem: Historians once portrayed medieval guilds as (i) _____ institutions that stifled innovation, but recent archival work suggests a more (ii) _____ picture: some guilds actively spread new techniques among their members.
explanation: Institutions that 'stifled innovation' are hidebound, rigidly attached to old ways. 'But' and the evidence that some guilds spread new techniques show the new picture is more nuanced, mixed rather than wholly negative. 'Damning' is the trap: it would agree with the old portrayal instead of qualifying it.

stem: Contrary to the popular belief that multitasking boosts efficiency, studies show that switching between tasks (i) _____ performance on each, because the brain must repeatedly (ii) _____ itself to new demands.
explanation: 'Contrary to the popular belief' that multitasking helps, the studies show switching degrades, or worsens, performance. The cause is the cost of each switch: the brain must reorient, readjust, itself to the new task. 'Enhances' simply restates the belief the sentence rejects.

stem: The physicist was notoriously (i) _____ in print, hedging every claim with qualifications, yet in private letters she stated her conclusions with a (ii) _____ that startled her correspondents.
explanation: 'Hedging every claim with qualifications' defines being cautious. 'Yet' signals that her letters were the opposite, and what startled correspondents was her bluntness, plain and direct statement. 'Reticence' and 'modesty' would continue the cautious manner rather than contrast with it, and 'dogmatic' contradicts the hedging.

stem: Because the central bank's announcements had become so (i) _____, investors learned to ignore them, and when the bank finally issued a clear warning, the markets were slow to (ii) _____.
explanation: 'Finally issued a clear warning' implies earlier announcements were not clear: they were equivocal, open to more than one reading. Having learned to ignore the bank, investors were slow to react. 'Candid' would give investors a reason to listen, and 'recover' makes no sense before any fall has been described.

stem: Coffee first reached many European cities not as a beverage of pleasure but as a supposed (i) _____, sold by apothecaries for headaches; within a century, however, it had become so (ii) _____ that few drinkers gave any thought to its medicinal reputation.
explanation: Being sold by apothecaries for headaches marks coffee as a supposed remedy, a cure. 'However' shows that its medical image faded as it became commonplace, an ordinary part of life. 'Luxury' is the trap: the sentence explicitly says coffee did not arrive as a 'beverage of pleasure'.

stem: The memoir's appeal lies in its (i) _____: the author neither excuses her youthful mistakes nor dwells on them for sympathy, recounting them with a (ii) _____ that some readers find almost clinical.
explanation: Neither excusing nor milking her mistakes means she tells them honestly, so the appeal is her candor, frankness. A tone 'almost clinical' is detachment, emotional distance. 'Warmth' and 'bitterness' are both emotional tones, the opposite of clinical, and 'sentimentality' is ruled out by her refusal to dwell for sympathy.

stem: Octopuses were long considered (i) _____ creatures, capable only of simple reflexes, but experiments showing them unscrewing jars and escaping from tanks have made that view seem (ii) _____.
explanation: 'Capable only of simple reflexes' defines a primitive creature. Clever feats such as unscrewing jars contradict that view, making it untenable, impossible to defend. 'Prescient' (showing foresight) would mean the experiments confirmed the old view, and 'ingenious' belongs to the new picture, not the old one.

stem: Rather than publicly (i) _____ the rival firm's product, as its combative chief executive had done with earlier competitors, the company quietly studied it and released a version that (ii) _____ its strengths while fixing its weaknesses.
explanation: A 'combative' leader's usual response would be to attack, so the company was expected to be publicly denouncing the rival. Studying the product and fixing its weaknesses means the new version incorporated its strengths. 'Ignoring' is tempting because 'quietly studied' contrasts with it, but nothing combative or public is involved in ignoring.

stem: The surgeon's insistence on washing her hands between patients was at first (i) _____ by colleagues as a needless ritual; only when her ward's infection rate fell far below theirs did they begin to (ii) _____ the practice.
explanation: Calling the practice 'a needless ritual' shows colleagues derided, or mocked, it. 'Only when' her results proved better did they begin to emulate, or copy, her. 'Adopted' is the trap: it belongs to the later stage, not the first reaction, and 'question' would not be a change of attitude.

stem: Children acquiring a language often (i) _____ its rules, saying 'goed' instead of 'went'; such errors, far from showing confusion, reveal that the child has (ii) _____ a general pattern and is simply applying it too widely.
explanation: 'Applying it too widely' restates overgeneralize, to stretch a rule beyond where it belongs. Such an error shows the child has internalized, truly absorbed, the pattern for forming the past tense. 'Memorize' is the trap: a child who memorized forms would say 'went', and 'ignore' contradicts applying the rule.

stem: Coral reefs occupy a (i) _____ fraction of the ocean floor, less than one percent, yet they shelter a (ii) _____ share of marine species, perhaps a quarter of the total.
explanation: 'Less than one percent' is a minuscule, extremely small, fraction. 'Yet' contrasts this with a quarter of all species, a disproportionate share, far larger than the area would suggest. 'Negligible' would echo the first blank rather than contrast with it.

stem: The conductor's interpretations were (i) _____ rather than reverent; she would change tempos and cut repeats whenever she felt a score dragged, and purists accused her of treating great works with (ii) _____.
explanation: Changing tempos and cutting repeats are bold liberties, so her interpretations were audacious, daring, rather than reverent. Purists would complain of irreverence, a lack of respect. 'Piety' repeats the 'reverent' quality she lacked, and 'indifference' does not fit a conductor who cared enough to reshape the works.

stem: Far from settling the dispute, the statute's wording proved so (i) _____ that two courts reading the same sentence reached opposite conclusions, and the legislature was eventually obliged to (ii) _____ the provision in an amendment.
explanation: Two courts reading one sentence in opposite ways shows the wording was ambiguous, open to more than one meaning. The fix for ambiguity is to clarify the provision. 'Explicit' would have settled the dispute, and 'enforce' is the courts' role, not something an amendment does to unclear wording.

stem: The excavation team was careful not to (i) _____ the significance of the single coin they found, since one object could easily have been dropped by a later traveler and offered only (ii) _____ evidence that the site had been a trading post.
explanation: The reason given, that one coin might have been dropped by anyone, is a reason for caution, so the team avoided overstating its importance. A single object offers only tenuous, weak, evidence. 'Understate' is the trap: the doubt about the coin is a reason to claim less, not a warning against claiming too little.

stem: Restorers today favor (i) _____ interventions, removing grime but adding as little new paint as possible, in contrast to their predecessors, who (ii) _____ repainted damaged passages to suit the taste of their own era.
explanation: 'Adding as little new paint as possible' defines minimal interventions. 'In contrast to' means the predecessors did the opposite and freely repainted passages to their own taste. 'Reluctantly' and 'rarely' would make the predecessors similar to today's restorers, removing the contrast.

stem: The neighborhood's transformation was less (i) _____ than residents had feared: rents rose, but slowly enough that most long-time tenants were able to stay, and many came to regard the new shops as a (ii) _____ addition.
explanation: Tenants were able to stay, so the change was less disruptive than feared. The positive tone continues: many saw the shops as a beneficial addition. 'Gradual' is the trap, since the change was in fact slow, so calling it 'less gradual than feared' reverses the meaning; 'intrusive' clashes with the relief the sentence describes.

stem: For decades the planet's rings were assumed to be as old as the planet itself. Recent measurements of their brightness, however, suggest that they are (i) _____, perhaps only a few hundred million years old, since ancient rings would long ago have been (ii) _____ by infalling dust. If this estimate holds, astronomers today are (iii) _____ to be observing a feature that may not last.
explanation: 'However' and 'only a few hundred million years old' show the rings are young compared with the planet. Their brightness is the evidence, so old rings would have been darkened by dust. Living during a passing feature makes astronomers fortunate. 'Primordial' (existing from the beginning) is the old assumption, and 'unlikely' contradicts the fact that they are already observing the rings.

stem: Economists distinguish unemployment that is (i) _____, lasting only while workers move between jobs, from unemployment that is structural, arising when workers' skills no longer (ii) _____ what employers need. The first is a normal feature of a healthy economy; the second is far more (iii) _____, since retraining a workforce can take years.
explanation: 'Lasting only while workers move between jobs' defines transitory, short-lived. Structural unemployment arises when skills no longer match employers' needs. Because retraining takes years, it is intractable, hard to solve. 'Benign' (harmless) is the trap: it describes the first kind, which the passage calls 'normal'; 'chronic' would describe the second kind, not the first.

stem: The dialect was long dismissed as a (i) _____ form of the standard language, riddled with errors. Linguists who studied it closely found instead that it was (ii) _____, governed by consistent rules of its own, and their work helped (iii) _____ its speakers, who had been taught to be ashamed of how they talked.
explanation: 'Riddled with errors' shows the dialect was dismissed as debased, a corrupted version. 'Instead' and 'consistent rules' show it is systematic. Work proving the dialect rule-governed would vindicate, or clear of blame, speakers taught to feel ashamed. 'Archaic' (old-fashioned) does not match the charge of errors, and 'embarrass' reverses the effect of the research.

stem: The movement's painters rejected the (i) _____ finish prized by the academies, leaving brushstrokes visible and edges rough. Critics at first took this as a sign of (ii) _____, as if the artists simply lacked skill; only later was the roughness understood as (iii) _____, a means of capturing fleeting light.
explanation: Rejecting the academies' finish in favor of visible strokes means the academies prized a polished one. 'As if the artists simply lacked skill' restates incompetence. 'Only later' brings the corrected view: the roughness was purposeful, a chosen means to an end. 'Arrogance' is not lack of skill, and 'accidental' would repeat the critics' mistake.

stem: Foresters once believed that wildfires were (i) _____ to every ecosystem and should always be suppressed. Decades of suppression, however, allowed dead wood to pile up, so that when fires did occur they were far more (ii) _____. Many managers now set small controlled burns, accepting minor damage in order to (iii) _____ catastrophe.
explanation: A belief that fires 'should always be suppressed' means fire was seen as inimical, harmful, to ecosystems. Piled-up dead wood is fuel, so later fires were more destructive, the 'catastrophe' managers now try to forestall, or prevent in advance. 'Frequent' is tempting, but extra fuel makes fires bigger, not more common, and 'invite' reverses the purpose of controlled burns.

stem: The symphony's premiere was a (i) _____: the audience whistled and walked out, and reviewers called it noise. Yet within a generation the work had become a (ii) _____ of the concert repertoire, and the very dissonances that once (iii) _____ listeners are now taught as models of orchestral color.
explanation: Whistling, walkouts and reviews calling it noise mark the premiere as a fiasco, a complete failure. 'Yet' turns to later success: the work became a staple, a standard item, of the repertoire. The dissonances 'once' affronted, or offended, listeners. 'Footnote' would mean the work stayed minor, and 'bored' does not match an audience angry enough to walk out.

stem: The defendant's lawyer did not (i) _____ the facts; instead she argued that the law under which her client was charged was so vague that no citizen could know what it forbade. The court, though ordinarily (ii) _____ to strike down a statute, agreed that this one failed the basic test of (iii) _____.
explanation: 'Instead' shows the lawyer argued about the law rather than disputing, or contesting, the facts. 'Though' requires the court's usual attitude to contrast with its agreement, so it is ordinarily reluctant to strike down laws. A law too vague to understand fails the test of clarity. 'Severity' is tempting, but the complaint is vagueness, not harshness.

stem: Brutalist buildings, with their raw concrete and massive forms, were for years (i) _____ as cold and forbidding, and many were demolished. Recently, however, a younger generation has come to admire their (ii) _____, praising the honesty with which they display their materials, and preservation groups now campaign to (iii) _____ the survivors.
explanation: Being called 'cold and forbidding' and torn down means the buildings were reviled, intensely disliked. 'Praising the honesty with which they display their materials' restates frankness. Preservation groups campaign to protect what remains. 'Ornament' is wrong for bare concrete, and 'disguise' would hide the very materials admirers praise.

stem: Memories feel like (i) _____ recordings of the past, but research shows that they are (ii) _____: each time we recall an event we rebuild it, and details can shift without our noticing. Eyewitness testimony, however (iii) _____ the witness may be, should therefore be treated with caution.
explanation: 'But research shows' contrasts the feeling with the fact, so memories feel accurate. Being rebuilt each time and shifting unnoticed means they are malleable, easily reshaped. 'However ... may be' introduces a quality that would normally earn trust, so the witness may be sincere and still wrong. 'Unreliable' fails because a concession needs a point in the witness's favor.

stem: Tariffs are often defended as a way to (i) _____ young domestic industries from foreign competition. Yet the protection can prove (ii) _____: sheltered firms, facing little pressure to improve, may grow so (iii) _____ that they cannot compete once the tariffs are removed.
explanation: 'Protection' and 'sheltered firms' show tariffs are meant to shield industries. 'Yet' introduces a drawback: firms with no pressure grow complacent, self-satisfied and unwilling to improve, so the protection proves counterproductive, defeating its own aim. 'Temporary' does not explain why the firms end up unable to compete, and 'efficient' reverses the effect.

stem: Some orchids attract pollinators through (i) _____ rather than reward: their flowers mimic the scent of a female wasp, so that males arrive expecting a mate and leave (ii) _____, having received no nectar. Because the trick works only if wasps cannot easily tell the difference, the orchids' mimicry must be remarkably (iii) _____.
explanation: Mimicking a female wasp is a trick, so the orchids rely on deception rather than reward. Males who get 'no nectar' leave unrewarded. A trick that fails if wasps can 'tell the difference' must be convincing. 'Satiated' (fully fed) contradicts 'no nectar', and 'crude' mimicry would be easy to detect.

stem: Early printed books were designed to look as much like manuscripts as possible, and printers (i) _____ the conventions of scribes, even copying their abbreviations. Only gradually did printers (ii) _____ these habits and develop a typography suited to the new technology, one that exploited the press's capacity to produce thousands of (iii) _____ copies.
explanation: Making books look like manuscripts and 'even copying their abbreviations' means printers imitated scribes. 'Only gradually' marks a change, so printers later shed those habits. The press's distinctive capacity is producing identical copies; hand-decorated, or 'illuminated', pages belong to the manuscript tradition, and thousands of 'unique' copies is a contradiction.

stem: Biologists had assumed that the songbirds navigated by the stars, but birds raised under (i) _____ skies found their way just as well, suggesting that the stars were (ii) _____ to their navigation. Further experiments pointed to a magnetic sense, though how the birds (iii) _____ the earth's field remains unclear.
explanation: 'But' signals that the test undermined the star theory, so the birds must have been raised without a view of the stars, under overcast skies. Navigating 'just as well' without stars shows the stars were incidental, not necessary. A magnetic sense requires that birds detect the field. 'Essential' is the old assumption the experiment disproved.

stem: The poet's (i) _____ was legendary; she published only two slim volumes in fifty years, revising each poem dozens of times. Admirers saw this as (ii) _____, a refusal to release anything less than perfect, while detractors called it (iii) _____, a fear of judgment dressed up as principle.
explanation: Revising each poem dozens of times shows fastidiousness, extreme care over details; 'prolificacy' contradicts two slim volumes in fifty years. 'A refusal to release anything less than perfect' is the admirers' positive reading, integrity. 'A fear of judgment' is the detractors' negative reading, timidity. 'Vanity' is negative, so it cannot be the admirers' view.

stem: Seismologists can say with some confidence where large earthquakes are likely, but not when; forecasts of timing remain so (i) _____ that public agencies tend to (ii) _____ them, focusing instead on building codes that make structures (iii) _____ to shaking whenever it comes.
explanation: Being unable to say 'when' means timing forecasts are unreliable. Agencies therefore disregard them, 'focusing instead' on building codes, whose purpose is to make buildings resistant to shaking. 'Publicize' would contradict 'instead', and 'vulnerable' reverses the purpose of a building code.

stem: Start-ups often (i) _____ larger rivals not because they have more resources but because they have fewer: without layers of management, they can (ii) _____ quickly when customers' needs change. As they grow, however, many acquire the very (iii) _____ that once slowed their competitors.
explanation: The sentence explains an advantage, so start-ups outmaneuver, outwit through quicker movement, larger rivals. Without management layers they adapt quickly. 'However' introduces the irony of growth: they gain the bureaucracy that slowed rivals. 'Agility' is the trap: it is what the start-ups had, not what slowed the competitors.

stem: The critic's praise was so (i) _____ that artists learned to discount it; a reviewer who called every exhibition 'remarkable' offered readers no (ii) _____ by which to tell genuine achievement from mere competence.
explanation: Calling every exhibition 'remarkable' is praise that is indiscriminate, given without distinguishing between cases. Such praise supplies no criterion, a standard for judging, that separates real achievement from competence. 'Incisive' (sharply perceptive) is the trap: perceptive praise would be worth trusting, and 'grudging' praise would not be handed to every show.

stem: Far from being (i) _____, the theory's predictions were hedged so carefully that almost any experimental outcome could be reconciled with them, a pliancy that its critics regarded not as a strength but as a symptom of its (ii) _____.
explanation: A theory that can be reconciled with 'almost any' outcome cannot be proved wrong, so 'far from being' points to falsifiable, capable of being tested and refuted. Critics see this pliancy as a sign of vacuity, emptiness: a theory compatible with everything says nothing. 'Robustness' is the defenders' reading, the 'strength' the critics reject, and 'ambiguous' agrees with the hedging instead of contrasting with it.

stem: Although the pianist's technique was (i) _____, her playing was faulted for a certain (ii) _____: every note was in place, yet listeners came away unmoved, as if they had heard an exercise rather than a performance.
explanation: 'Every note was in place' shows her technique was impeccable, flawless. 'Although' sets up a fault despite this: listeners were unmoved, so her playing had aridity, a dry lack of feeling. 'Gaucheness' (awkwardness) is a fault, but a technical one that contradicts the flawless technique; 'effervescence' (bubbly liveliness) would move listeners rather than leave them cold.

stem: The chronicler's account, once (i) _____ as the most reliable source for the reign, has lately come under suspicion; scholars note that it was written for the king's grandson and is (ii) _____ in its praise of the dynasty, passing over every defeat in silence.
explanation: 'Once' and 'has lately come under suspicion' show a fall in reputation, so the account was once prized as reliable; 'impugned' (attacked as false) describes the present view, not the past one. Written for the king's grandson and silent on every defeat, the praise is fulsome: excessive and flattering. 'Measured' would make the account more trustworthy, not suspect.

stem: The ecologist's warnings were neither (i) _____ nor equivocal: she conceded every uncertainty in her data, yet she refused to let uncertainty become an excuse for (ii) _____, since waiting for proof would mean waiting until the wetland was gone.
explanation: The colon explains the two denials in order. Conceding every uncertainty shows she was not dogmatic, asserting views as beyond doubt. Refusing to let doubt justify delay shows she was not equivocal; the excuse she rejects is for inaction, since waiting would cost the wetland. 'Tentative' and 'diffident' (lacking confidence) are near-synonyms of equivocal, and conceding uncertainty would not rule them out.

stem: Loanwords seldom keep their original meanings intact: a term borrowed for some (i) _____ purpose, such as naming a single dish or a legal procedure, often broadens until it is so thoroughly (ii) _____ that speakers no longer sense anything foreign about it.
explanation: Naming 'a single dish or a legal procedure' is a narrow, specialized purpose, and the word then 'broadens', which only makes sense if it began narrow; 'general' reverses this. A word whose foreignness speakers no longer sense is naturalized, fully absorbed into the borrowing language. 'Exotic' is the opposite, and 'obsolete' words are not used enough to broaden.

stem: The astronomer's notebooks reveal a mind far less (i) _____ than his published papers suggest. In print he presented each discovery as the inevitable result of method; in private he recorded false starts, (ii) _____ hunches and long stretches of bafflement, a record that makes his eventual success seem less (iii) _____ and more hard-won.
explanation: The papers present discoveries as 'the inevitable result of method', so the notebooks show him less methodical than that. Alongside false starts and bafflement, the hunches were inchoate, only partly formed. The private record makes success seem less foreordained, settled in advance, echoing 'inevitable'. 'Unerring' hunches would fit the published image, and 'laborious' means much the same as 'hard-won', so it cannot be its contrast.

stem: Advocates of the four-day work week insist that its benefits are not merely (i) _____, a matter of happier staff, but tangible for employers, citing trials in which output held steady. Skeptics counter that such trials are (ii) _____, since the firms that volunteer are presumably those best suited to the change, and that results from so (iii) _____ a sample cannot be generalized.
explanation: 'Not merely ... but tangible' needs a contrast with tangible, and 'happier staff' describes a benefit that is intangible, hard to measure. Firms that volunteer because they suit the change make the trials skewed, biased in one direction. Such a self-selected group is an unrepresentative sample. 'Premature' is a possible criticism, but the reason the skeptics give is about who takes part, not about timing; a 'randomized' sample is exactly what these trials lack.

stem: Because the painter destroyed most of her sketches, scholars must (i) _____ her working methods from the finished canvases alone, a task made more (ii) _____ by her habit of painting over earlier compositions. X-ray studies have begun to (iii) _____ this difficulty, revealing abandoned figures beneath the visible surface.
explanation: Without sketches, scholars must infer, reason out, her methods from indirect evidence; 'document' would require direct records, which were destroyed. Painting over earlier work hides evidence, so the task is more fraught, full of difficulty. X-rays that reveal hidden figures attenuate, or lessen, the problem. 'Compound' (make worse) reverses the effect of a technique that uncovers what was hidden.

stem: The island's flora is famously (i) _____: most of its species occur nowhere else. This uniqueness, however, carries a (ii) _____ cost, since species confined to a single small range have no populations elsewhere from which to recover, and conservationists thus regard the island's botanical richness as at once a treasure and a (iii) _____.
explanation: Species that 'occur nowhere else' are endemic, native to and restricted to one place; 'cosmopolitan' species occur worldwide. The danger is hidden until a disaster strikes, so the cost is latent, present but not yet visible. 'At once a treasure and' calls for a contrasting negative: a liability, a source of risk. 'Negligible' contradicts the warning, and nothing in the sentence concerns money.

stem: The composer's late quartets baffled his contemporaries, who heard in their abrupt shifts of mood only (i) _____, the incoherence of a mind in decline. Later listeners discerned a (ii) _____ logic beneath the apparent disorder, and the works once dismissed as (iii) _____ are now ranked among his most profound.
explanation: Abrupt shifts heard as 'incoherence' amount to caprice, sudden unpredictable change. The logic later found lay 'beneath the apparent disorder', so it was recondite, hidden and hard to grasp; a 'transparent' logic would have been obvious to contemporaries. Works blamed on a declining mind were dismissed as aberrations, departures from his normal standard. 'Pastiches' (imitations of others' styles) does not fit a charge of incoherence.

stem: The new regulation was meant to be (i) _____, applying only until the agency could study the problem; yet, as often happens with stopgap rules, it proved remarkably (ii) _____, and two decades later it remains in force, its (iii) _____ origins largely forgotten.
explanation: 'Applying only until the agency could study the problem' defines provisional, temporary. 'Yet' and 'remains in force' two decades later show the rule was tenacious, persistently long-lasting; 'ephemeral' (short-lived) is what it was meant to be. Its forgotten beginnings were expedient, chosen for convenience as a quick fix. 'Venerable' (respected for age) describes what it has become, not how it began.

stem: Dictionaries were once regarded as (i) _____ authorities whose rulings settled disputes about usage. Modern lexicographers disclaim this role, describing their work as (ii) _____ rather than prescriptive; yet readers persist in consulting dictionaries as arbiters, and the lexicographers' (iii) _____ has done little to change the habit.
explanation: Authorities whose rulings 'settled disputes' were seen as magisterial, speaking with commanding authority. 'Rather than prescriptive' calls for its contrast, descriptive, recording usage rather than ruling on it; 'normative' means much the same as prescriptive. 'Disclaim this role' is restated by disavowal, a denial of responsibility. 'Imprimatur' (an official stamp of approval) is the authority they reject.

stem: The cathedral's builders knew they would not live to see it finished, since construction took more than two centuries; their (i) _____ is all the more striking given how (ii) _____ the project seemed to contemporaries, many of whom mocked it as a folly. Today the structure stands as a monument less to any single architect than to collective (iii) _____.
explanation: Working for generations on a building they would never see shows tenacity, persistent determination. A project mocked as a folly seemed quixotic, idealistic and impractical. The monument honors the shared virtue that kept work going, steadfastness. 'Prudent' contradicts the mockery, and 'extravagance', though a charge critics might make, does not explain why the builders deserve a monument.

stem: The therapist's approach was (i) _____: rather than offering interpretations, she asked questions and let clients reach their own conclusions. Colleagues who favored more (ii) _____ methods considered her passive, but she argued that insights clients arrived at themselves were less likely to be (iii) _____ once therapy ended.
explanation: Guiding people by questions so that they reach their own conclusions is a Socratic approach; 'didactic' (instructive, lecturing) is its opposite. Colleagues who found her passive preferred directive methods, in which the therapist steers. Her argument is that self-found insight lasts, so it is less likely to be discarded afterward. 'Internalized' and 'cherished' reverse her claim, since she wants these outcomes to be more likely.

stem: The botanist was (i) _____ in the field, tramping through swamps in all weathers to collect specimens, but (ii) _____ at home: her herbarium was a jumble of unlabeled sheets, and only after her death did a curator, sorting patiently through the (iii) _____, discover several species new to science.
explanation: Tramping through swamps 'in all weathers' shows she was indefatigable, tireless. 'But' contrasts this with her home habits: a jumble of unlabeled sheets is slapdash, careless and hasty work. The curator sorted through that clutter. 'Meticulous' contradicts the jumble, 'careless' in the field would leave no contrast with her home habits, and a 'catalog' is what the collection lacked.

stem: Satire depends on a shared standard: the satirist mocks what an audience already recognizes as (i) _____. When a society's values are too (ii) _____ for any such consensus to exist, satire loses its target, and what was meant as ridicule may be read as (iii) _____.
explanation: Mockery works when the audience already sees its target as risible, deserving laughter. Without consensus, values must be fragmented, broken into separate camps; 'uniform' or 'stable' values would make consensus easy. Ridicule that misses its mark may then be taken as its opposite, endorsement, approval. 'Parody' is itself a form of ridicule, so it gives no misreading.

stem: Glass appears (i) _____, yet its molecules lack the orderly lattice of a crystal; this (ii) _____ structure once fed the popular claim that old windowpanes flow like a very slow liquid, a notion physicists have since (iii) _____, calculating that any such flow would take far longer than the age of the universe.
explanation: 'Yet' requires a contrast with lacking a crystal's lattice, so glass looks rigid, like an ordered solid; 'translucent' sets up no such contrast. A structure without an orderly lattice is amorphous, lacking definite form, and 'crystalline' contradicts the clause before it. Showing the flow would take longer than the universe's age means physicists debunked the claim; 'corroborated' reverses their finding.

stem: The ethnographer's early reports cast the community's gift exchanges as purely (i) _____, acts of generosity that expected nothing in return. Later fieldwork revealed an intricate (ii) _____: every gift created an obligation, and failure to repay was a source of lasting shame. The earlier account, in short, had mistaken a (iii) _____ system for spontaneous kindness.
explanation: 'Generosity that expected nothing in return' defines altruistic. Gifts that create obligations to repay form a system of reciprocity, mutual exchange. A system enforced by shame is binding, not 'spontaneous'. 'Voluntary' is the trap: it repeats the early, mistaken view, and 'hierarchy' is never mentioned in the evidence about repayment.

stem: The hypothesis was at first greeted with (i) _____, for it required the existence of matter that no telescope had detected. As observations accumulated that no rival theory could explain, however, resistance gave way first to grudging tolerance and then to open (ii) _____, until the once (iii) _____ idea had become the field's orthodoxy.
explanation: Requiring unseen matter would draw skepticism, and the later word 'resistance' confirms it. The sequence moves from resistance toward acceptance, so after grudging tolerance comes open advocacy, active support. An idea that became orthodoxy must once have been heterodox, contrary to accepted views. 'Canonical' describes where the idea ended, not where it began, and 'repudiation' runs backward along the sequence.

stem: The forecast had called for (i) _____ skies all weekend, so the hikers were caught unprepared when a (ii) _____ storm drove them off the mountain on Saturday afternoon.
explanation: Being 'caught unprepared' means the forecast promised good weather, clear skies. The storm surprised them, so it was sudden. 'Predicted' contradicts the hikers' surprise, and a 'gentle' storm would not drive anyone off a mountain.

stem: The teacher's explanations were so (i) _____ that even students who had struggled with the topic for weeks finally understood it, and several thanked her afterward for the (ii) _____ with which she went over the material again and again.
explanation: Explanations that finally made a hard topic understood are lucid, clear and easy to follow. Going over the material 'again and again' for struggling students shows patience. 'Confusing' reverses the result, and neither 'severity' (strictness) nor 'indifference' fits a teacher who kept repeating the material until it was understood.

stem: Sea otters may look (i) _____ as they float on their backs, but they are fierce predators whose appetite for sea urchins helps (ii) _____ kelp forests from being stripped bare.
explanation: 'But they are fierce predators' requires that otters look the opposite, harmless. Sea urchins strip kelp, so otters that eat urchins help save the forests. 'Dangerous' gives no contrast with 'fierce', and 'remove' kelp forests from being stripped makes no sense.

stem: Paper money was at first (i) _____ by merchants accustomed to gold and silver coins, but once they saw how much easier it was to carry, its use became (ii) _____.
explanation: 'At first' and 'but once they saw' its convenience signal a change of attitude, so merchants first distrusted paper money. After the change, its use became widespread. 'Welcomed' leaves no change for 'but' to mark, and 'rare' contradicts the merchants' new view.

stem: Ballet can look (i) _____, as if the dancers were floating through the air. In fact it demands enormous (ii) _____, and many dancers train for years before they can make the hardest steps appear (iii) _____.
explanation: 'As if the dancers were floating' describes something that looks effortless. 'In fact' reveals the hidden reality: ballet demands strength. Years of training let dancers make hard steps appear easy, matching the first sentence. 'Difficult' is the trap: dancers train to hide difficulty, not to show it.

stem: The researcher's findings were at first (i) _____ because they came from a single small study; only after three independent teams obtained (ii) _____ results did the field begin to accept them.
explanation: A single small study is weak evidence, and 'only after' implies early doubt, so the findings were discounted, given little weight. Acceptance came when other teams obtained consistent results, matching the original ones. 'Retracted' findings would not later be accepted, and 'contradictory' results would deepen the doubt.

stem: Silent-film actors relied on (i) _____ gestures and expressions, since they could not use their voices; when sound arrived, this style quickly came to seem (ii) _____, and actors had to learn a subtler manner.
explanation: Without voices, actors had to show feeling through exaggerated gestures. Once sound arrived and a 'subtler manner' was needed, the old style seemed overwrought, too intense and overdone. 'Restrained' and 'understated' are a trap pair: they describe the subtler manner that replaced silent acting, not silent acting itself.

stem: Early translation software produced sentences that were grammatically (i) _____ yet often absurd in meaning, because it matched words one by one without grasping (ii) _____; a sentence could be correct in every part and nonsensical as a whole.
explanation: 'Yet often absurd' and 'correct in every part' show the grammar itself was flawless. Matching words one by one ignores how surrounding words shape meaning, which is context. 'Syntax' (sentence structure) is the trap: the sentences were grammatically correct, so syntax was not the problem.

stem: The fossil was initially classified as a (i) _____ of a known species, since it differed only slightly from earlier specimens. A closer examination, however, revealed features so (ii) _____ that researchers now place it in a new genus, and its discovery has (iii) _____ debate about how the group evolved, since it fits none of the existing family trees.
explanation: Differing 'only slightly' from known specimens makes it a variant, a slightly different form, of the species. 'However' and a new genus show the features were distinctive. A fossil that 'fits none of the existing family trees' reignited debate. 'Settled' is tempting for an important find, but a misfit fossil raises questions rather than answering them.

stem: When the suspension bridge opened, many engineers considered its slender deck dangerously (i) _____. The designer, however, had tested models in wind tunnels and was (ii) _____ that the deck would hold, and a century of (iii) _____ service has proved him right.
explanation: A 'slender' deck that worried engineers was considered flimsy, too weak. 'However' and wind-tunnel testing show the designer was confident. Proof that he was right is a century of uneventful service, free of problems. 'Turbulent' service would support the engineers' worry, not the designer's judgment.

stem: The essayist's style is (i) _____, circling a subject from many angles and wandering through anecdotes before settling on a claim, and readers who prefer (ii) _____ argument, proceeding step by step from premise to conclusion, find her maddening.
explanation: Circling a subject and wandering through anecdotes define a discursive style, one that moves from topic to topic. Readers frustrated by it want the opposite, linear argument, which the sentence glosses as 'step by step from premise to conclusion'. 'Meandering' is the trap: it describes the essayist, so readers who prefer it would enjoy her, and 'terse' (brief and blunt) contradicts the wandering.

stem: The observatory's director was (i) _____ about announcing the unusual signal, insisting that her team first rule out every mundane explanation. Her (ii) _____ proved wise: the signal was eventually traced to a microwave oven in the staff kitchen, an outcome that would have been (iii) _____ had the discovery already been trumpeted to the press.
explanation: Insisting on ruling out every ordinary cause before speaking shows she was circumspect, cautious and wary. 'Her ... proved wise' refers to that same quality, restraint. A kitchen appliance revealed after a public announcement would have been mortifying, deeply embarrassing. 'Precipitate' (hasty) and 'alacrity' (eager speed) describe the opposite of her behavior, and 'inconsequential' ignores how damaging the false announcement would have been.

stem: The academy's apparent (i) _____, its willingness to admit any qualified painter, masked a subtler exclusivity: the entrance examinations were so (ii) _____ and costly that only the children of existing members could realistically prepare for them, so that the academy's celebrated (iii) _____ was more rhetorical than real.
explanation: 'Willingness to admit any qualified painter' defines openness, and 'masked a subtler exclusivity' shows it was only apparent. Exams that only insiders could prepare for were onerous, heavily burdensome; 'perfunctory' (done as a mere formality) would let anyone through. The celebrated but unreal quality is the same claim to openness, egalitarianism, belief in equal access. 'Parochialism' (narrowness) describes the reality the academy hid, not the image it celebrated.

stem: Fungi were long treated as (i) _____ organisms, mere decomposers of dead matter. It is now clear that many are indispensable partners of living plants, trading nutrients through root networks so (ii) _____ that some forests could not persist without them; the old view, in retrospect, was not merely incomplete but (iii) _____.
explanation: 'Mere decomposers' casts fungi as peripheral, of minor importance; 'pivotal' is the newer view. Networks on which whole forests depend must be intricate, richly interconnected, not sparse. 'Not merely incomplete but' calls for a stronger fault, misguided, wrong in its basic direction. 'Prescient' (showing foresight) would praise the old view the sentence criticizes.

stem: The playwright's dialogue seems at first (i) _____, a string of banal remarks about the weather and dinner; only gradually does the audience realize that each platitude is (ii) _____ with menace, and that what the characters leave unsaid is more (iii) _____ than anything they say.
explanation: Banal remarks about weather and dinner seem innocuous, harmless; 'sinister' is what the audience discovers 'only gradually', not the first impression. A platitude that hides menace is freighted with it, loaded with a heavy hidden meaning. The unsaid speaks louder than speech, so silence is more eloquent, expressive. 'Embellished' suggests open decoration, but the menace here is concealed, and 'trivial' contradicts the turn toward hidden meaning.
